# Focal seizures and syndromes

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Seizure disorders > Focal seizures and syndromes*

[Original Article Link](/library/iR0J5f)

---

## Summary

Focal (or partial) <u>seizures</u> are an abnormal activation of <u>neurons</u> confined to one cerebral hemisphere, and are best described according to whether or not consciousness and/or awareness are impaired. In contrast, <u>generalized seizures</u> are characterized by abnormal neuronal activity that quickly spreads to both hemispheres of the <u>brain</u>. <u>Seizures</u> can be caused by genetic abnormalities, structural abnormalities, metabolic disturbances, tumors, or infection. Symptoms depend on the location of the <u>ictal</u> event within the <u>brain</u> and may include clonic movements, as well as sensory and psychiatric symptoms. <u>Focal seizures</u> may involve altered <u>levels of consciousness</u> (<u>complex partial seizures</u>) or evolve to secondarily <u>generalized seizures</u>. <u>Temporal lobe epilepsy</u> is the most common type of <u>focal seizure</u>. It frequently arises from hippocampal <u>sclerosis</u>, but may also be caused by malignancies or infections. Diagnosis of <u>focal seizures</u> begins with <u>electroencephalography</u> and <u>neuroimaging</u>. If an infectious or a metabolic etiology is suspected, laboratory tests can also be helpful. <u>Focal seizures</u> secondary to underlying non-neurologic pathologies (e.g., infection or metabolic disturbances) are treated by correcting the underlying abnormality. <u>Seizures</u> of unknown etiology or from a neurological defect are managed with <u>antiepileptic drugs</u> such as <u>lamotrigine</u> (first-line), <u>levetiracetam</u>, or <u>phenytoin</u>.

---

## Etiology

### Common causes




* Genetic

* Structural and/or metabolic disturbances:

* Morphologic changes (e.g., hippocampal <u>sclerosis</u>, <u>tumor</u> growth)

* <u>Electrolyte</u> imbalances

* Drug intake

* Infections





#### Based on age group




* Childhood: <u>perinatal</u> injury to the <u>brain</u>

* <u>Adolescence</u>

* <u>Encephalitis</u>

* Cerebral trauma

* Middle-aged adults: cerebral tumors

* Adults of advanced age

* Vascular <u>encephalopathies</u>

* <u>Vascular dementia</u>

---

## Focal seizures with structural or metabolic cause

### Temporal lobe epilepsy




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: most common form of <u>epilepsy</u>

* ∼ 40% of all <u>epilepsy</u> cases

* ∼ 70% of focal <u>epilepsy</u> cases

* Etiology

* Hippocampal <u>sclerosis</u>: found in approx. 70% of patients suffering from <u>temporal lobe epilepsy</u> that is resistant to pharmacotherapy

* <u>Encephalitis</u> (e.g., <u>herpes simplex encephalitis</u>)

* Developmental disorders

* <u>Neurodegenerative disorders</u>

* Tumors

* Clinical features: <u>Seizures</u> commonly occur in <u>clusters</u>, last approx. 30 seconds to 2 minutes, and follow a specific sequence.  [[1]](/library/1la2Dk)
1. * <u>Aura</u>

* <u>Visceral</u>, olfactory, or auditory

* Feelings of familiarity or unfamiliarity and “dreamy states”
2. * Focal seizure with impaired awareness (<u>complex partial seizure</u>) 

* Motor symptoms 

* Typically oral alimentary <u>automatisms</u> (e.g., lip-smacking)

* Fidgeting (e.g., with clothing)

* Stretching of the body

* Walking in place

* Autonomic symptoms

* <u>Tachycardia</u>

* Urge to void the <u>bladder</u>

* <u>Mydriasis</u>

* Sweating, salivating

* <u>Altered mental status</u>

* Children appear absent-minded (e.g., staring ahead, unresponsive when spoken to)

* No <u>loss of consciousness</u>

* Less frequently: loss or change in the sense of <u>taste</u> or <u>smell</u>, <u>aphasia</u>

* <u>Focal seizures</u> may progress to <u>generalized seizures</u>.
3. * <u>Postictal phase</u>

* Confusion and tiredness (common)

* Transient <u>epileptic</u> <u>amnesia</u> (rare): anterograde or <u>retrograde amnesia</u> immediately preceding or following a <u>seizure</u>

* Diagnosis: <u>EEG</u> shows <u>temporal lobe</u> spikes

* Treatment

* Pharmacotherapy: e.g., <u>lamotrigine</u>, <u>levetiracetam</u>

* Surgical treatment: in case of medication resistance

* Prognosis: unfavorable (only 40% of patients on pharmacotherapy remain asymptomatic)

### Frontal lobe epilepsy




* Etiology: See “<u>Etiology of focal seizures and syndromes</u>” above.

* Clinical features

* Usually simple <u>partial seizures</u> featuring:

* Motor symptoms

* Muscle tension

* Vocalization

* Gaze deviation

* Head directed towards the unaffected side

* Autonomic symptoms (<u>enuresis</u>, salivation)

* Impairment of speech

* Attention deficits (staring spells that may appear similar to <u>absence seizures</u>)

* Jacksonian march

* Spreading of <u>paresthesia</u> or uncontrolled motor activity from one part of the body to adjacent areas, usually distally to proximally

* Results from <u>seizure</u> activity that progresses to the motor cortex

* March may progress to involve the entire limbs or the entire side of the body.

* <u>Todd's paralysis</u>: sustained <u>paralysis</u> of the affected limb/area after the <u>seizure</u>

* Usually a series of short <u>seizures</u> (≤ 30 s) occurring during <u>sleep</u> (which often wake the patient)

* No <u>aura</u>

* No <u>postictal</u> period of confusion





> [!TIP]
> <u>Focal seizures</u> that feature Jacksonian marches are termed Jacksonian <u>seizures</u>, regardless of the origin of the <u>seizures</u>.




### Parietal lobe epilepsy




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: 5% of cases of focal <u>epilepsy</u>

* Etiology: See "<u>Etiology of focal seizures and syndromes</u>" above.

* Clinical features

* Simple <u>partial seizures</u>, characterized by:

* Sensory symptoms (e.g., <u>paresthesia</u>, pains)

* <u>Dyslexia</u>

* <u>Sensory aphasia</u>

* Possible <u>Jacksonian march</u>

* Transition to temporal or <u>frontal lobe seizures</u> (featuring the respective symptoms) may occur.





### Occipital lobe epilepsy




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: rare

* Etiology: See "<u>Etiology of focal seizures and syndromes</u>" above.

* Clinical features

* Simple <u>partial seizures</u>, characterized by:

* <u>Visual hallucinations</u>

* Gaze deviation

* <u>Cortical blindness</u>

* Transition to temporal or <u>frontal lobe seizures</u> (featuring the respective symptoms) is possible.





> [!TIP]
> In general, patients suffering from <u>partial seizures</u> of structural or metabolic origin should be treated with <u>antiepileptic drugs</u> (e.g., <u>lamotrigine</u> or <u>levetiracetam</u>).




### Epilepsia partialis continua




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: rare

* Etiology: unspecific; current or past damage to the cortex (e.g., <u>scar</u> tissue, <u>encephalitis</u>, tumors)

* Clinical features

* Clonic muscle activity of a particular region of the body (partialis), e.g., mouth, finger

* Symptoms persist for several days (continua).

* Might be considered a focal <u>status epilepticus</u>

* Treatment: treat the underlying condition
